fluff.overview: Valiant Systems, working alongside Wunderland Enterprises, developed the Striker Light Tank to meet pressing demand for an affordable, mobile fire support platform. First produced in the early decades of this century, the design filled gaps in second-line and planetary defense formations that lacked access to heavier vehicles. Initial versions relied on conventional internal combustion power plants, limiting endurance and cross-country performance, but demand quickly outstripped Valiant's production capacity. A comprehensive redesign transitioned the chassis to fusion power and upgraded the weapons suite, creating a vehicle capable of sustained high-tempo operations. The Striker became a fixture in AFFS armored regiments and spread through alliance arrangements to Lyran formations. Limited sales to the Draconis Combine further extended its operational presence, establishing the type across much of the Inner Sphere as an affordable and reliable fire support asset.
fluff.capabilities:
The production Striker's primary armament is a Valiant Arbalest LRM-15 rack integrated with an Artemis IV fire control system, giving the vehicle effective long-range indirect fire capability suited to harassment, interdiction, and fire support missions. Two Valiant Javelin Streak SRM-2 launchers supplement the main battery, providing reliable short-range defense while conserving ammunition against small and fast targets. Four tons of ammunition distributed between the three launcher systems allows flexible munition selection, though sustained high-tempo operations demand careful resupply planning.

The InterFus 155 fusion power plant drives the Striker to a cruising speed of 54 km/h and a flank speed of 86 km/h, enabling rapid repositioning between fire positions. Valiant Scutum ferro-fibrous armor provides meaningful protection for a 35-ton chassis, though the vehicle is not designed for sustained close combat against heavier opponents. The wheeled drivetrain favors road operations and firm terrain. In rough or boggy ground, the Striker's performance lags behind tracked designs, limiting its utility in certain operational environments. The Wunderland XXXV-1 Series communications and targeting systems are adequate without being exceptional, with the Artemis IV integration representing the primary qualitative advantage over earlier configurations.
fluff.deployment: An improvised field conversion of the standard Striker chassis to limited amphibious capability, developed by former AFFS mechanics outside any formal procurement program. The hull sealing, fuel cell conversion, and secondary rocket artillery turret were assembled from salvaged components, making each example a unique improvisation. The 'Wet Striker' is encountered primarily among pirate bands and irregular forces operating in coastal and riverine environments, where its amphibious capability provides operational reach unavailable to conventional wheeled designs. One captured example remains on display at the Goshen War College.
fluff.history:
The origins of the Striker Light Tank lie in a pair of interrelated problems that confronted the Federated Suns throughout the early Succession Wars. The first was the shortage of affordable, mobile fire support platforms for planetary militia and second-line armored regiments. The second was the chronic inability of Valiant Systems of Johnsondale to meet procurement demands using internal combustion-powered designs that wore quickly under wartime operational tempos. Valiant and Wunderland Enterprises addressed both problems simultaneously. Their joint development program produced a wheeled chassis capable of fielding effective LRM fire support at a price point accessible to militia commands, and initial production absorbed every unit AFFS procurement officers could authorize. Despite this demand, the early Striker was never more than a workhorse. Its conventional engine limited range and reliability, and crews assigned to it rarely expressed enthusiasm. The vehicle's reputation rested on availability and maintainability, not on tactical performance.

This changed in the late Succession Wars as recovered technologies reached Valiant's engineering teams. The redesign initiated in the late 3040s was comprehensive, touching nearly every system on the chassis. Replacing the internal combustion engine with an InterFus fusion plant increased both speed and operational endurance. The Valiant Arbalest LRM-15, slaved to an Artemis IV fire control system, essentially doubled the effectiveness of the vehicle's primary battery against maneuvering targets. Valiant Javelin Streak SRM-2 launchers replaced the original short-range system, eliminating wasteful ammunition expenditure on missed shots. Valiant Scutum ferro-fibrous armor rounded out the package, giving the upgraded Striker a survivability margin its predecessors lacked entirely. The redesigned vehicle entered production in 3053 and drew immediate attention from procurement officers who had long regarded the Striker as an acceptable compromise rather than a genuine combat asset.

The FedCom alliance brought the Striker into Lyran formations in significant numbers, and production at Johnsondale expanded to meet combined demand. Valiant's practice of selling limited runs to the Draconis Combine generated sustained controversy within the Draconis March commands, whose tankers occasionally found themselves facing their own supplier's vehicles across the battlefield. The commercial logic was difficult to dispute. The arrangement provided Valiant access to Combine-developed electronics and stealth technology, investments that eventually returned value in the form of the 3061 Upgrade's Guardian ECM integration and the later Stealth configuration. The DCMS sales were never large enough to shift the balance of force, but they remained a political irritant for as long as the policy continued.

The Jihad inflicted serious damage on the Johnsondale facility and disrupted factory output for years. Base-model and 3053 Upgrade production ceased as Valiant concentrated surviving resources on the 3061 Upgrade line, which carried higher margins and continued to fill urgent AFFS orders. Field refits proliferated during this period as units stripped components from battle losses and improvised configurations suited to local shortages. The (Ammo), (Laser), (LRM), and (SRM) variants circulating today are largely products of this era of improvisation, standardized after the fact by AFFS technical teams who recognized the modifications as worth perpetuating. The Wet Striker stands as a more extreme example of the same improvisation ethic, a salvage conversion assembled outside any formal program and pressed into service against AFFS installations during the chaos of the Jihad period.

Post-Jihad recovery restored Johnsondale to production and introduced the Sealed variant as a deliberate response to the era's proliferation of WMD threats. The Stealth configuration, cleared for production in the Dark Age, represents the current production ceiling of Valiant's investment in the platform. Through more than a century of production across multiple chassis generations, the Striker has accumulated the kind of institutional presence that transcends tactical merit. Units from the Seventeenth Avalon Hussars RCT to Combine border garrison formations have fielded the type. Informal traditions have accumulated around individual vehicles, most famously the Gypsie Queen of the Ninety-ninth Avalon Armored Regiment, a vehicle that has been destroyed and rebuilt so many times that its identity is essentially a matter of faith. That such traditions exist at all says something about the Striker's place in Inner Sphere military culture: a vehicle common enough to be unremarkable and present long enough to become legendary.
